newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan may cut AWB grain imports due to high prices.
newsitem.headline: Japan may cut AWB grain imports due to high prices.

text.p: The Food Agency of Japan, growing increasingly frustrated with high offer prices of Australian wheat and barley, said on Tuesday it would reduce imports from the country if prices were not reduced.
Such a move would force the agency, which has traditionally been a stable buyer of grain from Australia, to become a more market-oriented buyer.

"We're known as a stable importer, and have in the past bought wheat and barley even if prices fluctuated wildly," an agency official said. "But we may be forced to become more market-oriented from now on," he said.
The Food Agency, one of the world's largest grain buyers, is Japan's sole importer of wheat, barley and rice.
The agency satisfies the country's needs through import tenders held every Thursday.
In the past two tenders, the agency did not buy some Australian grain as it intended to because prices were too high.
The agency had planned to buy from Australia 20,000 tonnes of Standard White wheat and 20,000 tonnes of Prime Hard wheat in the May 22 tender and 20,000 tonnes of feed barley in the May 29 tender.

"Frankly speaking, the AWB's (Australian Wheat Board) offer prices are too high now to accept. Prices should be much lower, considering the Chicago wheat market's price levels," said Shinichi Yahagi, director of the Food Agency's trade division.
"If the AWB fails to lower prices, we may cancel some imports," Yahagi said. He would not disclose the current offer prices of Australian grains.
Japan has complained to the AWB about the high prices and is waiting for Australia to respond, Yahagi said.
Behind the Food Agency's woes is the yen's fall against the dollar since early this year, which has weighed heavily upon the agency's purchasing power, other agency officials said.
In the fiscal budget for the current year ending March 1998, the Food Agency has been allocated 180.5 billion yen to buy about 6.04 million tonnes of wheat and barley.
The budget for grain imports was drawn up at an exchange rate of 107 yen to the dollar. On Tuesday afternoon, the dollar was trading at about 116.30 yen.
The Food Agency's financial division has been asking the trade division to become more price conscious and look for cheaper supplies, agency officials said.
Japan's other main suppliers of wheat and barley are the United States and Canada.
